Do you know what IRC is? Internet Relay Chat.

Using IRC, you can use XDCC which is eXtended DCC where DCC is Direct Client-to-Client.

It's downloading directly from someone else essentially and not from a swarm of clients (Peer-to-Peer).

However, most clients when using XDCC is a dedicated server for serving files (when it comes to piracy).

XDCC via IRC is like next-generation UseNet. UseNet requires a subscription to use for various reasons which means money. XDCC via IRC does not require that and is therefore free in comparison.

What I do is "simple":
1. Download kvIRC and install.
2. Go to Settings > Configure kvIRC > DCC > File Transfer and check "Automatically Accept" and set the download location (NOTE: ONLY DO THIS WHILE ACTIVELY MANAGING THE CLIENT. You don't want someone pushing you a virus and it auto-download.) Edit: Let me clarify that "check 'Automatic Accept'..." thing. Uncheck it when you aren't monitoring the program. It's dangerous to leave checked.
3. Connect to Abjects network.
4. Connect to the #moviegods or #beast-xdcc channels.
5. Send messages to the bots that manage the XDCC to have the files sent to me.

That's it. Purely as an example, I'd send this to receive Captain America: Civil War in 720p: 

/MSG [MG]-HD|EU|S|Shot XDCC SEND 887

That is sending a Private message to the bot [MG]-HD|EU|S|Shot requesting the bot to send package 887 via XDCC to me. Package 887 is Captain America: Civil War in 720p.

Some Notes:
1. For #moviegods and #beast-xdcc, you have to have a registered username with Abjects network. That's simple though. Join the network > send "/msg NickServ HELP" and follow the instructions. It doesn't require emails or anything.
2. To search for the messages needed to request files, join #mg-chat and #beast-chat respectively and use "!s <search terms>".

OR, you can use http://www.ixirc.net which isn't always up-to-date.

For reference, I've capped out a 400 Megabit/s down connection downloading four files at around 8 Megabytes per second each in a matter of a few minutes (these were 2-10GB files each).

Not all servers give that kind of speed (usually between 500 Kilobytes per second to 1 Megabyte per second on average for many), but since there are many servers, you can easily max out your download before maxing out their upload.

They also do TV shows, E-books, Programs, etc etc.

It's a lot to take in, but once it's setup to automate (there are ways in kvIRC to auto-log into networks and channels when you open the program), it's easy-peasy.

In fact, once you've used #moviegods long enough, it allows you to subscribe to shows and such for auto-downloading as soon as it's available.

There is an anime version for stuff like this. Go here for search (it's better than ixirc.net but only for anime): http://www.nibl.co.uk/bots.php and in kvIRC join Rizon network then #NIBL channel.

IPS = Intrusion Prevention System. What I use is Snort, on top of pfSense. Which segues into an explanation of how the rest of it works: pfSense edge router running on top of a virtual host with several configured virtual networks; relevant to this conversation are WAN, PIA1, LAN, and DMZ1. WAN and LAN operate as expected; PIA1 sits on top of WAN and is a VPN route to, of course, PIA. DMZ is a virtual network housing, among other things, my seed box, and anything on that network goes out through the VPN. Completed torrents drop to a directory that is an NFS mount to a server on the LAN; scripts handle copying files out of this directory into my main network shares.

I also have two configured WAPs, with one going out through the native WAN IP, and the other going out through the VPN, just for fun. Point being, though, all of this didn't really take long to set up, and between Snort's automated host blocking, host-based blocklists at the firewall level, and automatic blocklist updates at the seed box, all running through a VPN, I'm pretty well insulated, and it's all running on one server.

Yep, everything is running atop a virtual host, even the pfSense install. You just have to keep all of your virtual networks straight. To be fair, the main reason I started doing it that way was the ability to snapshot pfSense before doing an upgrade, because it had a nasty habit of going tits-up. But if you want to go physical, you can accomplish the same thing by just backing the whole shebang up to USB first.

Heck, if you wanted to do the exact same thing, but isolate the router as a standalone, you could just set up a separate network card in your pfSense machine with a direct drop to your virtual host, and pass VLAN-tagged traffic across that. Same/Same at the end of the day, really.
